clue.text: Win but be quiet about taking a tip

parts.note: P, for piano, is the musical direction meaning quiet
RE is the Latin-derived word for about or concerning
a vail is an old word for a tip or gratuity given to a servant

explanation.surface: Advice to a winner to keep quiet about having accepted a tip.
explanation.walkthrough: VAIL, an archaic word for a gratuity, is the one piece most solvers will not know; 'but be' and 'taking' are joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevail is to triumph or come out on top, a synonym of winning.

clue.text: Psephologist's concern on the beach

parts.note: psephology, the study of elections, takes its name from Greek psephos, the small stone the Athenians voted with, found on the seashore

explanation.surface: An election analyst at the seaside, worried about something.
explanation.walkthrough: A psephologist studies voting; the word comes from Greek psephos, a small stone the Athenians used to cast votes.
explanation.definitionFit: A small smooth stone found on a beach is the thing the Greek root psephos names.

clue.text: Prior a noble ? That's right

parts.note: an earl is a British nobleman
i.e., Latin id est, means 'that is'

explanation.surface: A question whether a monastic prior is a nobleman, answered yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prior' looks like a monk; it is the adjective meaning 'before'. 'That's' gives IE (that is).
explanation.definitionFit: Earlier means coming before in time, the same sense as prior.

clue.text: Can it be gross rage that makes him strike first ?

definitions.text: Can it be gross rage that makes him strike first

indicators.note: the question can it be asks whether these letters, reshuffled, become something else

explanation.surface: Wondering whether pure anger drives the one who throws the first punch.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of GROSS RAGE rearrange to the answer, and the whole clue also describes him: the one who strikes first.
explanation.definitionFit: An aggressor is the party who attacks first or starts the hostilities.

clue.text: Flat-topped — how sensible

explanation.surface: Something with a flat top is said to be a sensible design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'how' is a joining word between the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally, a level head is flat on top; figuratively, someone level-headed is calm and has good judgment.

clue.text: These sports have no solid basis

definitions.text: These sports have no solid basis

parts.words: These sports have no solid basis
parts.note: sports with no solid ground under them are those played in or on water, such as swimming or water polo

explanation.surface: A sceptic dismissing certain sports as groundless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No solid basis' sounds like a charge that the sports are unfounded; it literally means they take place on liquid rather than solid ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Sports held in water, like swimming and diving, are called water sports or aquatic sports.

clue.text: Topless girl's a fool

indicators.note: topless tells us the word loses its first letter, its top in a down clue

parts.note: a lass is a girl; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A girl going topless is a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: LASS (girl) loses its top letter, L; 'girl's' means 'girl is', and 'a' links.
explanation.definitionFit: An ass is a stupid person, a fool.

clue.text: Claudius making advances to Hamlet?

parts.note: Claudius is the brother of Hamlet's father, and a pawnbroker who makes advances of money is called by the same family title

explanation.surface: Claudius seemingly making a pass at Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: In the play Claudius is Hamlet's father's brother. A pawnbroker is called 'uncle' in old British slang, and pawnbrokers make advances (loans).
explanation.definitionFit: Claudius is the brother of Hamlet's father, and a pawnbroker lending money is called by that family title.

clue.text: Electric ray as a weapon

explanation.surface: An electric ray used as a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as a' is a joining phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The electric ray is a fish of genus Torpedo that numbs its prey with a shock; the self-propelled underwater missile was named after it.

clue.text: Score with toe perhaps to preserve one's wicket ?

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters given may be in some other arrangement

explanation.surface: Advice to a batsman: use your toe to score and protect your wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture misleads: a wicket is also a small gate, and wooden gates are painted with a tar-oil preservative. 'with' and 'to' are joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: To creosote is to treat timber with a tar oil that protects it, as you would a garden gate.

clue.text: Mimsy birds

parts.note: in Lewis Carroll's Jabberwocky the line runs 'All mimsy were the' creatures in question, imaginary birds

explanation.surface: A description of some flimsy-looking birds.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Jabberwocky from Through the Looking-Glass: 'All mimsy were the borogoves'. Humpty Dumpty explains these are thin, shabby-looking birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's nonsense poem pairs the adjective mimsy with these invented birdlike creatures.

clue.text: Graphic line

parts.note: the line plotted on a graph is the bend traced through the data points

explanation.surface: A vivid line of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Graphic' suggests vivid description, but here it means 'of a graph': the line drawn on one.
explanation.definitionFit: The plotted line on a graph is called its curve, even when straight.

clue.text: Learning about one French river

indicators.note: about signals that the word for learning goes around the other piece

parts.note: lore is traditional learning or knowledge
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Studying a French river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Loire is the longest river in France, flowing to the Atlantic at Saint-Nazaire.

clue.text: Size of hereditary factors in Porsena

indicators.note: in tells us one piece sits inside the name of the Etruscan king

parts.note: Lars Porsena was the Etruscan king in Macaulay's Horatius, so Porsena's first name is Lars
genes are the units of heredity

explanation.surface: A remark about how much of Porsena's size he inherited.
explanation.walkthrough: Lars Porsena of Clusium is the king Horatius held the bridge against in Macaulay's Lays of Ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Largeness is bigness, the extent or bulk of something, i.e. its size.

clue.text: Bronx cheers that give a performer the pip

definitions.text: Bronx cheers that give a performer the pip

parts.words: Bronx cheers that give a performer the pip
parts.note: a Bronx cheer is a rude noise blown with the tongue, the same as a fruit that has pips; to give someone the pip is old British slang for annoying them

explanation.surface: Jeers from the crowd that irritate an entertainer.
explanation.walkthrough: A Bronx cheer is the American name for a rude spluttering noise; British slang calls it after a soft fruit, and 'gives someone the pip' means annoys them, with a nod to the fruit's pips.
explanation.definitionFit: The rude noise of derision is called blowing a raspberry, a name from rhyming slang raspberry tart.

clue.text: Singularly tasty outcome of a capital shoot

definitions.text: Singularly tasty outcome of a capital shoot

parts.words: Singularly tasty outcome of a capital shoot
parts.note: a shoot named after a capital city, Belgium's, is a small green vegetable; 'singularly' tells us it is just one

explanation.surface: Praise for the remarkably tasty bag from an excellent day's shooting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital shoot' reads as a fine day of game shooting; it is a plant shoot named after the capital of Belgium. 'Singularly' means both remarkably and in the singular, one sprout.
explanation.definitionFit: A Brussels sprout is the edible bud of a cabbage relative, a vegetable named after the Belgian capital.

clue.text: Wise before the event in respect of trouble

indicators.note: trouble works as a verb: the letters of the phrase are stirred up and disordered

explanation.surface: Someone who foresaw trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' links; 'trouble' is the anagram signal for the letters of IN RESPECT, which rearrange to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone prescient has foreknowledge, knowing what will happen before it does.

clue.text: Bob went slowly but still wrote badly

parts.note: a bob was the old British shilling, abbreviated s
crawled means moved very slowly

explanation.surface: Someone named Bob moved slowly but still wrote poorly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a name; it is British slang for a shilling, written s in old money. 'but still' is a joining phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrawled means wrote in a hurried, untidy hand, i.e. wrote badly.

clue.text: Murphy's enemy a colourful Spanish pop-singer, we hear

parts.note: colorado is Spanish for coloured, especially red

indicators.note: we hear signals that the pop-singer's title is to be taken by its sound

parts.note: a Beatle is one of the four members of the 1960s pop group

explanation.surface: A colourful Spanish pop star said to be someone's enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Murphy' is slang for a potato, from its Irish association; the Colorado beetle devastates potato crops. BEATLE sounds like BEETLE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Colorado beetle is a notorious pest that strips potato plants, so it is the potato's foe.

clue.text: English door-fastener and French shoe-fastener

parts.note: a latch is the English word for a simple door fastening
et is French for and

explanation.surface: A list of two fastenings, one English and one French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and French' does not join two items; it means the French word for 'and', ET.
explanation.definitionFit: A latchet is an old word for a thong or strap that fastens a shoe or sandal.

clue.text: The general's swallowed his chewing-sweet with the vegetables

indicators.note: swallowed means one piece is taken inside the other

parts.note: Robert E. Lee was the Confederate general; Lee's gives LEES
gum is a sweet made for chewing

explanation.surface: A general gulped his gum along with the vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan has no 'Times'; the OCR added it. LEE'S (the general's) swallows GUM; 'with the' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Legumes are pod-bearing vegetables such as peas, beans and lentils.

clue.text: If jumpy, you'll find Flamborough Head hazardous

indicators.note: head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: risky means hazardous

explanation.surface: A nervous person finds the cliffs at Flamborough Head dangerous.
explanation.walkthrough: Flamborough Head is a chalk headland on the Yorkshire coast, but 'Head' here takes just its first letter, F. 'If' and 'you'll find' are joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: Frisky means lively and inclined to leap about, so restless or jumpy.

clue.text: Loss of rights needs to gain revolutionary backing

parts.note: to attain is to gain or achieve

indicators.note: backing tells us the word for revolutionary is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: a Red is a communist revolutionary

explanation.surface: A political slogan: you will lose your rights unless revolutionaries back you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like support; it turns RED into DER. 'needs to' is a joining phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Attainder was the forfeiture of civil rights and property imposed on someone condemned for treason or felony.

clue.text: One medicine-man is a giant

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
Dr is the abbreviation for doctor, a medical man

explanation.surface: A tribal healer turns out to be enormous.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR read 'a' as '8'. Idris is the giant of Welsh legend whose chair is the mountain Cadair Idris.
explanation.definitionFit: In Welsh legend Idris Gawr is a huge man who sat on the mountain named after him.

clue.text: Smith, take a fresh- (Calverley)

parts.note: a quotation to complete: the Victorian poet C. S. Calverley wrote an ode to tobacco in which Smith is offered another smoke

explanation.surface: A line of verse with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan prints the gap as a dash and exclamation mark: "Smith, take a fresh——!" The line is from Calverley's Ode to Tobacco, and the missing word is something you smoke.
explanation.definitionFit: The line offers Smith another rolled tobacco leaf to smoke, which completes the quotation.

clue.text: Franz is not entirely battle-hardened

indicators.note: not entirely says only part of the hyphenated word is used, a run of letters inside it

explanation.surface: A man named Franz described as somewhat battle-hardened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is the link; the composer's surname sits across the hyphen of 'battLE-HARdened'.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Lehár was the Hungarian composer of the operetta The Merry Widow, so Franz is his first name.

clue.text: It is more superficial than beauty, even

definitions.text: It is more superficial than beauty, even

parts.words: It is more superficial than beauty, even
parts.note: the saying goes that beauty is only skin deep, so the outer layer of skin itself is shallower still

explanation.surface: A remark about something even shallower than good looks.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue turns on the proverb 'beauty is only skin deep': the top layer of skin is more superficial still.
explanation.definitionFit: The epidermis is the outermost layer of the skin, lying on the surface of the body.

clue.text: Thousands in the river?

explanation.surface: A question about thousands of something in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so thousands are Ms, spelt out as letter names; 'in the' is a joining phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The letter M stands for a thousand, so several are 'ems'; the Ems is a river in north-west Germany.

clue.text: Loathes taking notes at trials

parts.note: D and E are two notes of the musical scale
tests are trials or examinations

explanation.surface: Someone who hates taking notes during trials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'notes' gives two letters, D and E, two musical notes; 'taking' and 'at' are joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest is to hate intensely, a synonym of loathing.

clue.text: Content in this the actor is good enough

explanation.surface: Praise for an actor who gives a satisfactory performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in this the actor' means: put the word into 'the actor ...' and 'the actor satisfies' means he is good enough.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to content someone is to please them, and a thing that is good enough meets the requirement; both senses fit.
